# Diversification and Portfolio Theory {#chap-portfolio}  
  
A money or investment manager uses markets, options pricing, and  
financial data analysis to develop a strategy that best achieves  
financial goals — maximizing returns subject to limiting risk and  
providing adequate liquidity over a given time period. A trader seeks  
to implement a given strategy with maximum efficiency and minimum  
cost.  
  
## Managing Portfolios  
  
The view that investment strategies involve picking the right stock is  
naive. More important is constructing and managing portfolios of  
sizable numbers of different securities, and adjusting the weighting  
to accomplish different objectives. Often messy factors outside pure  
risk-return come into play, such as (1) tax liabilities and  
(2) liquidity/market impact.  
  
Both Markowitzian portfolio theory and the simplified CAPM relate  
returns on an asset to its level of risk, where risk is associated  
with the variance or volatility of the investment. Returns from a  
risk-free investment such as U.S. Treasury bills are guaranteed but  
fairly low; expected returns from more volatile investments such as  
stocks are higher, but so is the variance. The theory assumes  
investors are risk-averse: they take riskier investments only if  
expected returns are higher.  
  
## Types of Risk Revisited  
  
As discussed in Chapter \@ref(chap-risk), portfolio risk partitions  
into **systematic** (market) risk and **specific** (unsystematic)  
risk. Specific risk — e.g., will a company's management underperform —  
can be diversified away by buying a variety of assets, since specific  
risks cancel out. Systematic risk — e.g., will the central bank raise  
interest rates — cannot.  
  
## Volatility and Value  
  
If several stocks have the same expected return, we are better off  
owning all of them than one of them, because we remove specific risk:  
expected return is unchanged but portfolio variance is lower, so the  
combined portfolio is superior for a risk-averse investor.  
  
If assets A and B have the same expected return but A is more volatile  
than B, B is more desirable — which implies A must offer a higher  
expected return (lower price) to attract investors. Volatility also  
impacts option prices, since volatile assets are more likely to change  
significantly in value over time.  
  
## Diversification in Theory and Practice  
  
The theory assumes the risk-return profile of a portfolio can be  
optimized: an optimal portfolio displays the lowest possible risk for  
its level of return. Since adding a new asset further diversifies the  
portfolio, the optimal portfolio in theory contains all possible  
assets appropriately value-weighted. There is an optimal portfolio for  
any desired rate of return, because we can always invest some fraction  
of capital at the risk-free rate and the rest in an optimal portfolio  
at a higher rate.  
  
Such diversification explains why stock index funds outperform  
individual stock holdings, and why much of the difference in  
investment managers' performance reflects variable outcomes in  
specific risk more than skill. In practice, about 15 well-selected  
stocks can provide much the same diversification as a market index.  
  
## Uncorrelated Returns  
  
To maximize diversification, select securities whose performance is  
uncorrelated or, even better, negatively correlated.  
  
::: {.example #ex-seasonal name="Seasonal stocks"}  
Suppose stock A returns 20% in summer/fall and 0% in winter/spring,  
while stock B returns 0% in summer/fall and 20% in winter/spring. Each  
stock has a 10% expected return with high variance, but because they  
are perfectly negatively correlated, buying half of each gives a 10%  
return with zero variance.  
:::  
  
Unfortunately, all asset returns tend to become correlated in a  
crisis.  
  
## Portfolios of Two Stocks  
  
Suppose there are only two stocks, IBM and Merck, offering expected  
returns of 1.49% and 1.00% respectively, with variances of 0.007770  
and 0.003587. By adjusting the portfolio weight $w_1$ devoted to IBM  
(with $w_1 + w_2 = 1$), we can modulate expected return to any value  
between 1.00% and 1.49%. Portfolio variance changes as a function of  
the weights and the covariance between the two stocks' returns:  
  
\begin{equation}  
\sigma_p^2 = w_1^2\sigma_1^2 + w_2^2\sigma_2^2 +  
             2 w_1 w_2\,\mathrm{Cov}(R_1, R_2)  
(\#eq:twostock)  
\end{equation}  
  
Figure \@ref(fig:frontier) plots the opportunity set generated by  
Equation \@ref(eq:twostock) as $w_1$ varies (assuming  
$\mathrm{Cov}(R_1,R_2) = 0.001$ for illustration).  
  
```{r frontier, fig.cap="Two-asset opportunity set for IBM and Merck, assuming covariance 0.001."}  
w1 <- seq(0, 1, by = 0.01); w2 <- 1 - w1  
mu1 <- 0.0149; mu2 <- 0.0100  
s1 <- 0.007770; s2 <- 0.003587; cov12 <- 0.001  
  
mu_p  <- w1 * mu1 + w2 * mu2  
var_p <- w1^2 * s1 + w2^2 * s2 + 2 * w1 * w2 * cov12  
  
plot(sqrt(var_p), mu_p, type = "l",  
     xlab = "Portfolio standard deviation",  
     ylab = "Expected return")  
points(sqrt(s1), mu1, pch = 19); text(sqrt(s1), mu1, "IBM", pos = 4)  
points(sqrt(s2), mu2, pch = 19); text(sqrt(s2), mu2, "Merck", pos = 4)  
```  
  
## Portfolios with Short Sales  
  
Returns higher than the highest individual asset are possible with  
short sales: sell short the lower-return asset and use the proceeds to  
buy the higher-return one. Like leverage (borrowed money), the  
tradeoff is increased risk.  
  
## The Portfolio Frontier  
  
Note that one can earn a higher return than Merck at less risk in a  
portfolio. The **frontier** describes the space of optimal portfolios;  
the best point on it depends on one's appetite for risk, i.e., the  
utility function. Adding more securities can only improve the  
frontier.  
  
## The Frontier with a Risk-Free Asset  
  
When a risk-free asset exists, each portfolio consists of the  
risk-free asset and risky assets. Viewing the risky assets as a  
sub-portfolio, this sub-portfolio should lie on the optimal frontier.  
In fact, linear combinations of the **tangency portfolio** and the  
risk-free asset dominate the portfolio frontier.  
  
::: {.theorem #thm-tangency name="Tangency portfolio"}  
With a risk-free asset, all optimal portfolios are combinations of the  
risk-free asset and a single risky portfolio — the tangency portfolio  
— regardless of the investor's risk aversion.  
:::  
  
## The Capital Market Line  
  
The efficient set of portfolios combining the risk-free asset and the  
tangency (market) portfolio is the **capital market line** (CML):  
  
\begin{equation}  
E(R_p) = R_f + \frac{E(R_M) - R_f}{\sigma_M}\,\sigma_p  
(\#eq:cml)  
\end{equation}  
  
Equation \@ref(eq:cml) prices *portfolios* on the efficient frontier  
in terms of total risk $\sigma_p$, whereas the SML  
(Equation \@ref(eq:sml)) prices individual securities in terms of  
systematic risk $\beta_i$.
